description:
Hi! I'm Kanchana S Valmiki, and our team, Moonshot Mappers, is building a map to find places on Earth that are like the Moon and Mars.

I'm interested in space, maps, and data, and I'm eager to learn coding and research along the way.

Our project helps NASA practice for future Moon and Mars bases. We'll compare things like temperature, ground type, and terrain, then show which places on Earth are the closest match on an easy map
summary:
Moonshot Mapper is a single-page web app built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.” It helps teams find places on Earth that resemble candidate lunar and Martian base sites, so technology and crews can be tested there.

You choose a target: the Moon’s south pole (Shackleton rim), Mars Jezero, or Mars Arcadia Planitia. The app compares it with 12 Earth candidates, including Atacama, Haughton Crater, Death Valley, Deccan Traps, Ladakh and Iceland. Each site gets a 0–100 similarity score for mean temperature, terrain relief, albedo and aridity. Four sliders set the weights, which feed a weighted total. The results appear as a ranked table and colored map markers. Selecting a site shows each variable’s value, source and uncertainty note.
details:
What it does and how it works

Moonshot Mapper is a single-page web app that ranks Earth locations by how closely they resemble candidate Moon and Mars base sites. You pick a target (the Moon's south pole Shackleton rim, Mars Jezero crater, or Mars Arcadia Planitia), adjust sliders for how much each variable matters, and read the ranking. A table and colored markers on a Leaflet map update live. Each site is scored 0 to 100 on four variables: mean temperature, terrain relief, albedo, and aridity. The similarity formula is 100 × (1 − |Earth − target| / range), and the total is a weighted average using your slider weights. Users can also inspect the values, sources, and uncertainty behind each variable.

Benefits

Gives teams a quick, transparent way to compare analog test sites.

Shows how each score is built, so results can be questioned and tuned.

Needs no install or backend, and works on mobile.

Swapping in real data requires changing only one JSON file.

Intended impact

The goal is to help researchers and mission planners choose Earth test sites for Moon and Mars base technology with less guesswork. Few places on Earth resemble these targets, so a good choice saves effort. The app is meant as a screening tool that narrows candidates before deeper study.

Tools and technology

HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with Leaflet for the map. All data sits in one JSON block, and everything runs in the browser, so no special hardware or server is required. The current values are placeholders, to be replaced with NASA, USGS, and ESA data.

Creativity

It turns a hard planetary-science question into an interactive "what matters most to you?" tool. Because the weights are adjustable, different teams can explore different priorities instead of getting one fixed answer. Putting the whole model in a single editable data file also makes it easy to extend.

Factors the team considered

Transparency: a simple scoring formula that anyone can follow.

Comparability: ranges are measured across all candidate sites plus the target, so each variable sits on the same scale.

Honest limits: Earth can't reproduce gravity (9.81 vs. Mars 3.71 and Moon 1.62 m/s²), radiation, or vacuum. The app has a Limitations panel beside the results.

Scope: geology, mineralogy, ice, regolith, and illumination are not yet scored.

Data quality: the sample output (best match for Shackleton: Mauna Kea) uses placeholder data and equal weights.

Next steps: add the missing variables, expand beyond 12 candidate sites, show uncertainty ranges, and validate with domain experts.
